item.title: These Popular Books Suck
item.dc:creator: Jarosława Radowski
item.content:encoded:
And What You Should Read Instead

Instead of 48 Laws of Power by Robert Greene…

Read anything by Robert Caro.

Robert Caro writes comprehensive case studies on power, which highlights the level of ingenuity and effort powerful individuals go through. Don’t read instructional bullshit written by hustlers. Caro also highlights the importance of prose, saying that nonfiction needs to be well-written as well as well-researched. His works are the epitome of biography, and it’s no wonder he wins a Pulitzer for anything he writes.

I don’t think reading Working belongs in this category. If you watch and read a lot of his interviews, you will already know most of his stories.

Instead of Meditations by Marcus Aurelius…

Read Essays by Seneca (the younger).

Marcus Aurelius tends to get hyped up, but his Meditations were simply a couple of notes to himself to go through life as a stoic. It is not the best way to get introduced to stoicism, even if you read the prologue. I think Seneca is more accessible and philosophical. Read his essays before his letters.

Instead of King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild…

Read Congo: The Epic History of a People by David Van Reybrouck.

The former is written by a journalist who proclaims to be a socialist. His politics definitely affects how he interprets history. This generally happens with most mainstream works written by non-historians, such as Iris Chang’s The Rape of Nanking. Unlike The Rape of Nanking, there is a more credible work to refute the non-historian. Reybrouck’s Congo is comprehensive and more fair, and by far absolutely impressive.

Instead of 50 Shades of Grey…

Read Little Birds by Anaïs Nin.

You can never go wrong with Anaïs Nin if you need literary erotica. I know her book Delta of Venus is more popular, but there’s a bit more taboo fetishes in that book. Nin is where art and pornography intersects, and this book is a good introduction to her.

Instead of Goodnight Punpun by Inio Asano…

Read No Longer Human by Osamu Dazai

To be honest, I think Goodnight Punpun is overhyped. I suppose it does capture that sense of adolescent loneliness, but I personally related to the protagonist in No Longer Human more, and I considered the latter much more darker. I admit my decision may be colored by bias, but this book captured my childhood and young adulthood better than any other literary book aside for the fact that I am not an alcoholic playboy.

Instead of The Art of War…

Read Romance of the Three Kingdoms translated by Moss Roberts.

Like most of the books on this list, I think The Art of War is overhyped. There several interesting lessons you can take from there, but it’s difficult to retain them without case studies / examples.

Romance of the Three Kingdoms is worth reading only for Zhuge Liang. He only comes in like the second-ish(?) volume of the story, but his brilliance and strategems in this epic narrative just keeps you reading. He does have some deus ex machina moments, but those were mostly minimal in my memory.

Honestly this book is not easy to read, as a lot of nuance is lost in translation, Chinese characters share a lot of similar names, and there are hundreds of characters that end up backstabbing each other. But Zhuge Liang redeems it a bit.

Instead of The Da Vinci Code by Dan Brown…

Read Foucault’s Pendulum by Umberto Ecto.

There’s so much to hate about The Da Vinci Code and so much to love about Foucault’s Pendulum. It can be a hard read as its scope is encyclopedic, but if you’re patient and willing to put in the research while you read along, it can be very rewarding. I don’t usually recommend Foucault’s Pendulum as it’s sort of niche, and to be honest the main reason why it’s here is because I hate Dan Brown.

Instead of Hillbilly Elegy by J. D. Vance…

Read What You Are Getting Wrong About Appalachia by Elizabeth Catte.

This book essentially refutes the propaganda that J. D. Vance espouses, and she does so with nuance. Unlike J. D. Vance, Catte actually grew up and lives in Appalachia. Therefore this an actual insider’s views about the issues undergoing within the region even if there is an academic lens attached to it.

item.title: A Tale for the Time Being
item.dc:creator: Jarosława Radowski
item.content:encoded:
A Book Review

Did you know Meyers’ Twilight novels are bestsellers in China? It’s published with detailed footnotes explaining cultural references (slumber parties, Ivy League colleges, Greek mythology) that sometimes take up more than half a page. But under that veneer of cultural exchange, Twilight is still literary garbage.

I feel similarly about this book. The most it can provide is a cultural experience into a Japanese adolescent, as it is an inversion of the immigration / assimilation trope in Asian American women’s literature. But other than that, Ozeki doesn’t pull anything new within the genre.

Because parts of the novel is based on the narrations of a diary, this book fails to break the trope of Show, Don’t tell. Readers, just like Ruth, are told of what characters do (Jiko is a monk) and are (Haruki #1 is honorable) but there really isn’t much to read in between the lines. Consequently when Ruth is told of the characters’ endings, it comes off as Deus ex machina. Ironically, this gave Nao’s parents rather than Nao’s grandmother the greatest potential but the character development (much like the plot) meanders and flounders.

This also causes a disconnect between the characters and the readers. We’re told of Haruki #1’s decision to become a kamikaze pilot despite being a non-suicidal pacifist but this feels less of an emotional loss when Tae-yul does the same deed for similar reasons in Linda Park’s When My Name Was Keoko.

I also take issue with verisimilitude. As the titular quarterback star at my high school, I had my fair share of wedging otakus and knocking lunch trays off the hands of my kohais. But the idea that delinquents crashed a toilet stall to film a girl on her period, upload the video on the internet, steal her soiled underwear, and sell it online is a bit too over the top especially for a book that takes itself so seriously it contains footnotes and appendices. Stephen King’s Carrie has the protagonist pelted with tampons and sanitary napkins which is just as humiliating and far more authentic.

Throughout the book Nao goes through some incredibly horrific abuse but she psychologically handles the trauma like water off a duck’s back. Her tone remains chummy and upbeat, and and the most we see is suicidal ideation. I don’t deny depression can be hidden by cheery facades, but all nuance is lost when we’re just repeatedly told of Nao being depressed rather than being shown trichotillomania or self-mutilation. This is the complete opposite to Osamu Dazai’s No Longer Human in which the narrator’s self-destructive behaviors are bellied by self-loathing and guilt but he vaguely mentions his childhood molestations in a single sentence.

I’m all for intellectual stimulation but incorporating science and spirituality is rarely done well. In here, it comes off as cringeworthy and pretentious, especially how much it’s squeezed in the last chapter. There are great philosophical discussions within science, but you enter the realm of pseudoscience and not metaphysics when you try to justify supernatural phenomena with quantum mechanics.

That is not to say this novel is hopeless. I’ve mentioned the cultural tidbits, from Buddhist aphorisms and local slang. I enjoyed the dream sequences. Overall this is an adequate metafictional novel with a gorgeous cover. Starts off strong before it tumbles haphazardly into the sea but boy does it take its time to kamikaze.

There are better written works that evocatively relate to Japanese psyche on emasculation and suicide, with themes of modernization vs tradition in Soseki’s Kokoro and Murakami’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle.

Rating: 2/5

item.title: How To Approach Conflict
item.dc:creator: Jarosława Radowski
item.content:encoded:
Five simple advices for self-actualization in face of adversity

  1. When you approach any political / ethical question, you have to start from the foundation that your opponent is trying to do something that they think is a moral good. 99% of people are good and decent people.
  2. When faced with a person, ideology, or system that you dislike, Instead of analyzing it and figuring out what you don’t like about it and move on from there, the natural inclination is to do the exact opposite of what that idea is. Do not define your entire ideology by the opposition; do not be just a reactionary.
  3. Our brain is not a reliable observer or narrator. It is so many different biases that affect the type of memories you form, the things you remember when you do research, the things you look for when you do research. There are two checks you could perform to ensure you’re not in an epistemic bubble: know the best argument against your stance, and know what would change your mind on your stance. Brains might be bias by nature, but you can detect bias by nuture.
  4. People’s feelings can be irrational sometimes, but they are never random. Even trauma responses are based on a particular stimuli that someone was exposed to earlier to life. People can have beliefs that don’t track onto data, but sometimes people confuse this phenomenon to randomness or maliciousness. People’s feelings may be irrational but never random. There is a specific reason why they believe in what they believe. It’s our job to find that out to convince them otherwise.
  5. You can’t change the world, but you can change your world. The most we can do is to establish the locus of control with us and to not externalize that. Do everything to maximize your happiness; a happy foundation of a person is going to be better able to deal with and change and impart their values on the world.

item.title: How Democracies Die: What History Reveals About Our Future
item.dc:creator: Jarosława Radowski
item.content:encoded:
A Book Review

A good read on the modern rise of authoritarianism: how it occurs through case studies around the world, how it is happening to America, and what America can do to prevent it.

Overall, I found it thoroughly researched and well written by scholars and yet accessible for the masses. This isn’t a comprehensive or definitive account of the erosion of democracy, but that’s not exactly what the book was going out to prove. Most of the negative reviews of this book are due to different expectations. So beware: this book is trying to explain Trump, and I believe it accomplishes those aims.

If you’re wondering why there is an absence of American-backed coups like Chile and Iran, it’s because Trump did not gain power through military force. The writers are not being political, they’re being succinct and relevant to their thesis. The introduction specifically clarifies this discrepancy.

Which brings up the point… Going into this book expecting its agenda to be political is to turn the gun on yourself. A woman who says, “All men are trash” reveals more about herself than on men. There are negative reviews that call out the authors for being Clinton apologists or elitists blind to the wealthy. Well, the joke’s on you, because the authors were being consistently apolitical.

There are criticisms for Trump, obviously, but they also do not condone actions taken by Obama, FDR, and even Lincoln. Some of the advice for Democrats in the concluding chapter is very similar to what Republican strategist Rick Wilson suggests in Everything Trump touches dies.

Explanations of history are not equivalent to solution proposals. In a discussion about democratic gatekeeping, the authors bring up that party leaders made backroom deals to take full advantage of the electoral college. Not only is this obsolete — the authors even pinpoint when and how — but also the exact opposite of what the book is advocating for. The conclusion clearly calls for more democratization, and democratic gatekeeping is only utilized to explain establishment politicians who embrace extremists legitimizes them to the public.

I wish the world’s problems can be waved away by removing a singular entity, whether they are immigrants, the wealthy, or some other boogeyman. Unfortunately reality is far more complex and this sort of conspiratorial thinking is far less nuanced than what the book delves into. I can’t help but wince when others beat down the knowledge within this book with their own anecdotes and political beliefs.

This was written by political theorists interested in institutional dysfunction not the socioeconomic climates that ferments government upheavals. Keep all this in mind, manage your expectations reasonably, and you can enjoy and appreciate this book with an open mind.

Rating: 4/5
